T0: Welcome, I'm glad you're here! When you press the button on a torch and the light comes on straight away, what do you think is happening inside it?

T1: A battery is what pushes charge round a circuit. Charge is the tiny particles in a wire that carry electricity, and you can't see them. What would you see happen to a torch bulb if charge started flowing through it?
[side picture after T1: none; newest in the chat: none]

T2: That's fine. Here's a hint: you can't see the charge itself, but you can see what it does. Think of a torch: you press the button, charge starts flowing through the bulb, and something happens to the bulb straight away. What does the bulb do?

T3: Yes, that's right. In a circuit, a bulb is called a lamp, and it lights because charge is flowing through it. A flow of charge is called an electric current, and its size is how much charge passes a point each second.

T4: Picture a running track: the runners are the charge, and the current is how many runners pass one spot on the track each second. Now imagine twice as many runners passing that spot each second. What would happen to the size of the current?
T5: Yes, that's right. Twice as many runners passing each second means twice the current, and that rate of flow is what current measures.
T6: Current has its own unit, the ampere (A, or amps), which measures how much charge passes a point each second.
T7: The charge itself is counted in coulombs (C), and one ampere means one coulomb passing a point each second. So a bigger current means more coulombs passing each second.
T8: The ammeter is the meter that measures current in amperes, and it goes in the loop itself, so the charge passes through it.
T9: Picture a runner-style count: a current of 3 A means 3 coulombs of charge pass a point every second. A current of 1 A is a smaller flow than that.

T10: Inside the metal wire are tiny particles that carry electric charge, the thing that flows round a circuit. When the circuit is switched on, these particles all start to drift round the loop together, like runners setting off round a track at the same moment.
[T10 told piece: model, 45 words, key point 1]
T11: A complete loop of wire, with no gaps anywhere, is called a closed circuit. Like a running track, it brings charge back to where it started, so the same charge can keep going round and round.
[T11 told piece: model, 36 words, key point 1]

T12: A closed circuit alone is not enough. The loop also needs something to push the charge round, and that is a cell, the part that pushes charge round a circuit. Join two or more cells together and you have a battery. Without a cell or a battery in the loop, the charge just sits still.
[T12 told piece: model, 55 words, key point 1]

T13: A switch is a part that opens or closes a gap in the loop, on purpose, to stop or start the flow. Flick it off and there is a gap in the track, so the charge stops everywhere. Flick it on and the loop is complete again.
[T13 told piece: model, 47 words, key point 1]
[side picture after T13: "A closed circuit: a cell, a switch and a lamp in one loop."; newest in the chat: picture "A closed circuit: a cell, a switch and a lamp in one loop."]

T14: In a single loop, the current is the same at every point. Charge is not used up on the way round, so the same amount passes each point every second. Wherever you put the ammeter, the meter that measures current, it reads the same.
[T14 told piece: model, 44 words, key point 1]
[side picture after T14: "The same loop with an ammeter in it, measuring the current."; newest in the chat: picture "The same loop with an ammeter in it, measuring the current."]

T15: Charge flow, written Q, is the total amount of charge that passes a point, counted in coulombs (C). Current tells you how fast the runners pass each second, while charge flow is the whole crowd that has passed after some time. The longer the current runs, the more charge flows past.
[T15 told piece: model, 51 words, key point 1]
T16: The equation is Q = I t: charge flow = current × time. Q is the charge flow in coulombs (C), I is the current in amperes (A) and t is the time in seconds (s).
[T16 told piece: equation, 36 words, key point 1]

T22: An electric current is just charge moving round a circuit, like runners going round a track. The more runners passing a point each second, the bigger the current. Picture a track where twice as many runners pass a point each second as before. What has happened to the current?

S23 (ask): is that the same as charge

T23: The same: charge is what moves (the runners), and current is how fast it moves, meaning how much charge passes a point each second. If fewer runners pass a point each second on the track, what has happened to the current?
T24: Yes, that's right. Current is the rate of charge flow, so fewer runners passing each second means a smaller current.
T25: In one line, in your own words: what is an electric current?
T26: Your line gets the key idea right: a current is a flow of charge, and you've said it moves round the circuit. Nothing important is missing.
T27: Quick question: You open the switch in a single loop. What happens to the current?
S28 (ask): why does it stop everywhere
T28: Yes, that's right. Break the loop anywhere and the flow stops everywhere.
T29: Connect a lamp to one cell and it glows dimly, then add a second cell and it glows brighter. That means more current is flowing, so the cells must be doing something extra to the charge.
T30: The extra push from each cell is called potential difference: the push that drives charge through a part of the circuit. It is measured in volts (V), and people often call it voltage.

T31: Potential difference is the push on the charge, so a bigger push means more charge flowing through the lamp each second. Think of the two cells making the runners on the track push harder. If you used three cells instead of two, what would you expect to see happen to the lamp's brightness?
T32: Yes, that's right. Brighter is right: more cells means more push, so more current.
T33: A voltmeter is the meter that measures potential difference, and it is connected across the part you are testing, not in the loop.

[side picture after T33: "The same loop with a resistor added, and a voltmeter connected across the lamp."; newest in the chat: picture "The same loop with a resistor added, and a voltmeter connected across the lamp."]
T34: Volts (V) are the unit that measures potential difference, the push on the charge. A cell with a bigger push, in volts, drives more current round the circuit.

T35: Another name for potential difference is voltage, and the exam may use either word, so both get the mark. Now picture a lamp in a loop with one cell, and you want to measure the potential difference across the lamp. Where does the voltmeter go?

T36: Voltage is just another word for potential difference, the push on the charge. You can say either one in an exam. A voltmeter measures that push across a part of the circuit, so which meter would you use to find the voltage across a lamp?
T37: Yes, that's right. The voltmeter is the meter that measures the potential difference across a part of the circuit, such as a lamp.
T38: Back to my question: Where does the voltmeter go?
T39: Yes, that's right. Now the second thing that decides the current: resistance, how much a component opposes the current through it.
T40: Picture the lamp glowing in its loop of wire. Now add a resistor, a part that limits the current, into the same loop. The lamp dims again, because less current flows round the circuit.
[T40 told piece: model, 34 words, key point 2]

T41: From here on, the word component means any part of a circuit. The lamp is a component, and so is the resistor you just added. Whenever you see component, think of whichever part of the loop we are looking at.
[T41 told piece: model, 40 words, key point 2]

T42: Potential difference is the first thing that decides the current: the push that drives charge through a component. Picture the runners on their track. A lamp with two cells glows brighter because the push across it is bigger.
[T42 told piece: model, 38 words, key point 2]

T43: Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the symbol Ω. An ohm is the unit that tells you how strongly a component opposes the current through it. A component with a bigger number of ohms makes it harder for charge to get through, like a narrow, bumpy stretch of the running track.
[T43 told piece: model, 52 words, key point 2]

T44: Keep the push the same and change only the resistance. Potential difference stays fixed, but a component with a bigger resistance makes it harder for charge to get through, so less current flows. On the running track, the same push sends fewer runners past a point each second when the track is narrower and bumpier.
[T44 told piece: model, 55 words, key point 2]

T45: The equation linking potential difference, current and resistance can be rearranged. Know any two of the three and you can work out the third. For example, with the potential difference and the resistance, you can find the current by dividing the potential difference by the resistance.
[T45 told piece: model, 46 words, key point 2]

[T45 shown first: The equation is V = I R: potential difference = current × resistance. V is the potential difference in volts (V), I is the current in amperes (A) and R is the resistance in ohms (Ω).]
